```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 5
)
```

# Why parameter uncertainty matters

A single calibrated run gives one trajectory per variable, and it looks far more
certain than it is. Many process parameters -- light extinction, mixing
coefficients, inflow and outflow scaling, the biogeochemical rate constants --
are only loosely constrained by the data we have. Several quite different
parameter vectors can reproduce the observed temperature profile equally well and
then diverge when asked about oxygen, or about a season that was not observed.

Running the model over an **ensemble of parameter sets** makes that visible. The
spread across members is a direct, model-based estimate of how much of the
prediction is controlled by what we do not know about the parameters. It is one
axis of uncertainty alongside the initial state (see
`vignette("initial-conditions-and-spin-up")`) and the forcing.

This article covers three things:

1. **running an ensemble** with `run_aeme_ensemble()`, here with parameter sets
   sampled from each parameter's `[min, max]` range;
2. **supplying calibrated sets** -- in particular the posterior from a PEST++
   iterative ensemble smoother calibration;
3. **writing the output to Parquet**, so a large ensemble can be stored compactly,
   queried without loading it all, and compared with other ensembles later.

```{r setup, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(AEME)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

options(AEME.inform = FALSE)
```

We use the example lake shipped with the package, simulated with GLM-AED.
Copy its configuration somewhere writable, load it, and build the model once:

```{r build, message = FALSE, results = "hide", warning = FALSE}
tmpdir <- tempdir()
path <- file.path(tmpdir, "lake")

aeme_file <- system.file("extdata/aeme.rds", package = "AEME")
aeme <- readRDS(aeme_file)
```

# The parameter table

An ensemble needs something to vary. AEME describes calibratable parameters in a
long data.frame with one row per parameter: the `model` and `file` it lives in,
its `name`, a current `value`, and the `min` and `max` that bound it. The package
ships a ready-made table:

```{r params}
data("aeme_parameters", package = "AEME")
param <- aeme_parameters[aeme_parameters$model == "glm_aed", ]
as.data.frame(param[, c("file", "name", "value", "min", "max")])
```

The example lake has no parameters attached, so we attach the table to the `aeme`
object with `add_param()`. The `min`/`max` columns are the sampling space, so
this is the place to encode what you believe about each parameter. The shipped
`Kw` range (light extinction) runs from 0.1 to 5.5 m<sup>-1</sup>, which spans
everything from clear alpine water to a bloom; for this lake we narrow it:

```{r attach-params}
param$max[param$name == "light/Kw"] <- 1.5
aeme <- add_param(aeme, param)
```

Then build the GLM-AED configuration:

```{r build-model, message = FALSE, results = "hide", warning = FALSE}
aeme <- build_aeme(aeme, model = "glm_aed", path = path, ext_elev = 3)
```

# A sampled ensemble

`run_aeme_ensemble()` runs a model once per **parameter set** you give it. For
each member it writes the parameters into the model configuration with
`input_model_parameters()` and then calls `run_aeme()`, and it stores every
member's output on the returned object under `output(aeme)$ens_001 ... ens_00k`.
A member that fails is dropped, with a warning, and the rest are renumbered.

`param_sets` is either

- a **list of parameter data.frames**, one per member, each with the `value`
  column set; or
- a single **long data.frame** with an `ensemble` id column plus the usual
  parameter columns.

Each data.frame has the same columns as `parameters(aeme)`; only `model`, `file`,
`name` and `value` are required.

The simplest ensemble draws each parameter independently and uniformly between
its `min` and `max`. That is a few lines of R, so we write it ourselves:

```{r sample-sets}
sample_param_sets <- function(param, n) {
  sets <- lapply(seq_len(n), function(i) {
    p <- param
    p$value <- runif(nrow(p), p$min, p$max)
    p
  })
  setNames(sets, sprintf("m%02d", seq_len(n)))
}

set.seed(42)
param_sets_prior <- sample_param_sets(parameters(aeme), n = 12)
head(param_sets_prior[[1]][, c("name", "value", "min", "max")])
```

Then run them:

```{r run-sampled, message = FALSE}
aeme_prior <- run_aeme_ensemble(aeme, model = "glm_aed", path = path,
                                 param_sets = param_sets_prior)
output(aeme_prior)$n_members
```

Each parameter is sampled **independently**, so there is no correlation structure
between parameters, and every member is a complete model run. Swap in a normal
distribution, a Latin hypercube or anything else by changing how `value` is
filled -- `run_aeme_ensemble()` only sees the finished sets.

Members are independent, so they parallelise cleanly. Set `parallel = TRUE` (and
optionally `ncore`) to run them on several cores, each worker in its own copy of
the model directory:

```{r run-parallel, eval = FALSE}
param_sets_prior <- sample_param_sets(parameters(aeme), n = 100)
aeme_prior <- run_aeme_ensemble(aeme, model = "glm_aed", path = path,
                                 param_sets = param_sets_prior,
                                      parallel = TRUE, ncore = 4)
```

## Members that fail

Some combinations of parameters are simply unphysical for a lake -- for example
an outflow scaling that drains the lake faster than the inflow fills it. GLM does
not report that as an error: it exits normally, the water level goes to zero and
below, and the rest of the output is `NA`. `run_aeme_ensemble()` therefore checks
each member's water level and, by default (`drop_incomplete = TRUE`), drops any
member whose level reaches zero or goes `NA`, as well as any that error or
produce no output. The warning above names the members dropped, and the survivors
are renumbered `ens_001`, `ens_002`, ...

Because the sets were named, the labels of the survivors are kept:

```{r screen}
kept <- attr(output(aeme_prior), "realisation")
kept
setdiff(names(param_sets_prior), kept)
```

Comparing the dropped members' parameters with the survivors' shows what went
wrong. Here the inflow and outflow scalings are the usual culprits:

```{r screen-why}
bind_rows(param_sets_prior, .id = "member") |>
  filter(name %in% c("inflow", "outflow")) |>
  mutate(status = ifelse(member %in% kept, "kept", "dropped")) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(id_cols = c(member, status), names_from = name,
                     values_from = value) |>
  arrange(status, member)
```

Set `drop_incomplete = FALSE` to keep every member, `NA`-padded after the model
stopped, if you want to inspect them. A tight parameter range, or a supplied
ensemble that has already been through a calibration, is the best way to avoid
failures in the first place.

## Summarising and plotting

`plot_ensemble()` shows the central interval of the ensemble as a ribbon, with
the lake observations overlaid, for one variable and depth:

```{r plot-ribbon, warning = FALSE}
plot_ensemble(aeme_prior, model = "glm_aed", var_sim = "HYD_temp", depth = 1,
              conf_int = 0.95)
```

`type = "line"` draws one line per member instead, which is useful for seeing
whether the spread comes from a few outlying members or from the ensemble as a
whole:

```{r plot-lines, warning = FALSE}
plot_ensemble(aeme_prior, model = "glm_aed", var_sim = "HYD_temp", depth = 10,
              type = "line")
```

Extracting a variable from every member is the slow part of both plots. If you
want several variables or depths, extract once with `ensemble_summary()` and
hand the result to `plot_ensemble()`:

```{r summary, warning = FALSE}
s <- ensemble_summary(aeme_prior, model = "glm_aed",
                      vars_sim = "HYD_temp", depths = c(1, 10))
s
head(as.data.frame(s))
```

# Supplying your own parameter sets

Sampling from the bounds answers "what if I only know each parameter lies
somewhere in this range?" Often you know more than that. A calibration leaves you
with parameter vectors that are already consistent with observations, and you
want to propagate *those* through the model. That needs no new function: the same
`param_sets` argument takes them.

Here we build a small set by hand: twelve members scattered around the current
values with a standard deviation of 10 % of each parameter's range, clipped to the
bounds. This stands in for what a calibration would give you:

```{r supplied-build}
set.seed(1)
param_sets <- bind_rows(
  lapply(seq_len(12), function(i) {
    p <- parameters(aeme)
    p <- p[p$model == "glm_aed", ]
    p$value <- pmin(pmax(rnorm(nrow(p), p$value, 0.1 * (p$max - p$min)),
                         p$min), p$max)
    p
  }),
  .id = "ensemble"
)
head(param_sets[, c("ensemble", "name", "value", "min", "max")])
```

```{r supplied-run, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
aeme_post <- run_aeme_ensemble(aeme, model = "glm_aed", path = path,
                                param_sets = param_sets)
output(aeme_post)$n_members
```

If the ensemble ids are named (as here), the surviving ids are kept on
`attr(output(aeme_post), "realisation")`, so you can map `ens_001`, `ens_002`, ...
back to your own labels after any failed members are removed.

```{r plot-supplied, warning = FALSE}
plot_ensemble(aeme_post, model = "glm_aed", var_sim = "HYD_temp", depth = 1)
```

## The posterior from a PEST++ calibration

The most useful thing to supply is the **posterior ensemble** from a
`pestpp-ies` calibration. An iterative ensemble smoother does not return a single
"best" parameter set: it returns a whole ensemble of parameter vectors, each of
which fits the observations, and the spread among them reflects how well the data
constrain each parameter.
`aemetools::pest_posterior_params()` turns that ensemble into a `param_sets` list
that `run_aeme_ensemble()` can run directly.

```{r pest, eval = FALSE}
# a finished pestpp-ies calibration -- see the aemetools "staged-calibration"
# vignette for how to set one up
calib <- aemetools::read_calib(ctrl = cal_ctrl, sim_id = cal_id)

post <- aemetools::pest_posterior_params(calib)
post

aeme_post <- run_aeme_ensemble(aeme, model = "glm_aed", path = path,
                                param_sets = post, parallel = TRUE)
plot_ensemble(aeme_post, model = "glm_aed", var_sim = "HYD_temp", depth = 1)
```

Some details worth knowing:

- Every set is **complete**. Parameters that were held fixed during the
  calibration (frozen in an earlier stage, or with `value == min == max`) are
  carried through from the calibration's parameter metadata, because the smoother
  only holds the adjustable ones.
- `iteration = 0` returns the **prior** ensemble instead, so you can run both and
  compare the prior and posterior predictive spread:
  `pest_posterior_params(calib, iteration = 0)`.
- `n_max` keeps only the first few realisations for a quick look at a large
  ensemble, and `include_base = TRUE` also keeps the `base` realisation (the
  initial parameter values).

The workflow of the whole calibration is described in the
[aemetools repository](https://github.com/limnotrack/aemetools).

# Writing the output to Parquet

An ensemble is big: every member holds every variable at every layer and every
timestep. A 100-member ensemble of a multi-year run is awkward to keep as an
`.rds` -- it all has to be loaded to use any of it. AEME can instead write the
output to a **Parquet** store with `write_aeme_parquet()`. Parquet is a compact,
columnar format that R, Python, DuckDB and most data tools read natively, and
`arrow` can query it without reading it all into memory.

```{r parquet-write, warning = FALSE}
pq_prior <- file.path(tmpdir, "parquet_prior")
write_aeme_parquet(aeme_prior, out_root = pq_prior, depths = c(1, 10))
```

The `depths` argument says where to summarise depth-resolved variables such as
temperature -- here 1 m and 10 m below the surface. It is explained under
*Depth-resolved variables* below; without it the summary tier is only really
useful for variables with no depth dimension.

(`write_aeme_parquet()` needs the `arrow` package.) The store is
[Hive-partitioned](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/r/articles/dataset.html), so
each lake and model has its own directory:

```{r parquet-tree}
list.files(pq_prior, recursive = TRUE)
```

There are two tiers of output per model:

| Tier | Contents | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| `output_raw` | Every member's series: `date`, `ens`, `var_sim`, `depth`, `value` | Drill-down into one lake -- spaghetti plots, per-member checks |
| `output_summary` | Ensemble `mean`, `sd`, `n_ens` and quantiles (`q05`, `q25`, `q50`, `q75`, `q95`) per `date`/`var_sim`/`depth`, with a `depth_ref` column saying what `depth` is measured from | Overview views, many lakes at once, without recomputing the collapse |

`output_summary` is only written when there is more than one member. The
`quantiles` argument sets which quantiles are stored, and `compression` chooses
the Parquet codec: `"gzip"` (the default) is smallest, `"snappy"` is fastest to
read and write, and `"zstd"` sits between them.

A one-row-per-lake table, `lakes.parquet`, records what was exported, including
how many ensemble members each lake has:

```{r parquet-lakes}
read_aeme_parquet(pq_prior, what = "lakes")
```

## Reading it back

`read_aeme_parquet()` filters by `lake_id`, `model`, `var_sim` and `date_range`
**before** reading, so asking for one variable never touches the others on disk.
For a scalar variable such as lake level the summary tier is all we need, and the
ribbon can be drawn without re-running or even loading the model:

```{r parquet-summary, warning = FALSE}
lvl <- read_aeme_parquet(pq_prior, what = "output_summary",
                         var_sim = "LKE_lvlwtr")
head(lvl)

ggplot(lvl, aes(date)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q05, ymax = q95), alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q25, ymax = q75), alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = q50)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Water level (m)") +
  theme_bw()
```

### Depth-resolved variables

Variables with a depth dimension need a little more care. AEME interpolates
GLM's own layers onto a standard grid when it loads the output, but that grid is
a set of *fractions of the water depth* scaled to the lake level on each day,
not a fixed set of depths. Members whose water level differs -- as the inflow and
outflow parameters make them -- therefore report slightly different depths on the
same date (on one day, eight members gave seven different depths for the same grid
point, 1.60--1.90 m), and each member's depths drift as its level moves.
Collapsing across members *at those depths* would leave most groups holding a
single member. The raw tier keeps the stored depths as they are, but for the
summary tier `write_aeme_parquet()` takes `depths`: each member's profile is
interpolated to those depths on every date, and only then are the members
collapsed. We asked for 1 m and 10 m when we wrote the store, so every member
contributes at both depths:

```{r parquet-depth, warning = FALSE}
temp_prior <- read_aeme_parquet(pq_prior, what = "output_summary",
                                var_sim = "HYD_temp")
head(temp_prior[, c("date", "depth", "depth_ref", "mean", "q05", "q50", "q95",
                    "n_ens")])
table(temp_prior$depth, temp_prior$n_ens)
```

`n_ens` counts the members that have a value. A depth that falls outside a
member's water column on a date -- deeper than that member's lake, or above its
surface -- is left out for that member rather than guessed at, so `n_ens` drops
below the ensemble size there.

`depth_ref` chooses what `depths` is measured from. The default, `"surface"`,
is metres below the water surface. With `"bottom"` it is metres *above the lake
bed*, so `depths = 1` is the water 1 m above the bottom. That is a different
height below the surface on every date and for every member, because the
water level differs, so it is worked out from each member's own level
(`LKE_lvlwtr`):

```{r parquet-bottom, warning = FALSE}
pq_bottom <- file.path(tmpdir, "parquet_bottom")
write_aeme_parquet(aeme_prior, out_root = pq_bottom, depths = 1,
                   depth_ref = "bottom")

bottom <- read_aeme_parquet(pq_bottom, what = "output_summary",
                            var_sim = "HYD_temp")
head(bottom[, c("date", "depth", "depth_ref", "mean", "q50", "n_ens")])
```

The raw tier is unchanged by `depths` and `depth_ref`: it always holds the
stored depths, in metres below the surface.

For a big store, push the filter into the Parquet scan with `collect = FALSE`,
which returns a lazy `arrow` query. Further `dplyr` verbs are applied before any
data is pulled into R:

```{r parquet-lazy, warning = FALSE}
ds <- read_aeme_parquet(pq_prior, what = "output_raw", var_sim = "HYD_temp",
                        date_range = c("2021-01-01", "2021-01-31"),
                        collect = FALSE)
class(ds)[1]

ds |>
  filter(!is.na(value)) |>
  group_by(ens) |>
  summarise(mean_temp = mean(value), n = n()) |>
  collect()
```

## Comparing ensembles

Because a store is just files, keeping several ensembles side by side is
straightforward. One thing to watch: the partitions are keyed by `lake_id` and
`model`, so re-exporting the same lake to the same `out_root` **replaces** its
data. Write each ensemble you want to keep to its own `out_root`.

Here we export the narrower, supplied ensemble to a second store and compare it
with the one sampled from the full parameter ranges:

```{r parquet-compare, warning = FALSE}
pq_post <- file.path(tmpdir, "parquet_post")
write_aeme_parquet(aeme_post, out_root = pq_post, depths = c(1, 10))

temp_post <- read_aeme_parquet(pq_post, what = "output_summary",
                               var_sim = "HYD_temp")

both <- bind_rows(prior = temp_prior, narrowed = temp_post, .id = "ensemble")

ggplot(both, aes(date, fill = ensemble, colour = ensemble)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q05, ymax = q95), alpha = 0.25, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(aes(y = q50)) +
  facet_wrap(~ paste(depth, "m"), ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Temperature (°C)", fill = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw()
```

The width of each band is the output uncertainty attributable to the parameters.
Two cautions when reading this particular plot. The narrowed ensemble is only a
tighter scatter around the current values, not a calibration, so it need not be
narrower everywhere. And the wide ensemble lost the members that drained the lake
(see *Members that fail*), so its band is built from fewer members than were
sampled.

With a real calibration the comparison is the point: store the `iteration = 0`
prior and the final posterior of a PEST++ run the same way. Where the posterior is
clearly narrower, the data have constrained what the model can do.

Size on disk for the twelve sampled members, with both tiers and every output
variable written:

```{r parquet-size}
files <- list.files(pq_prior, recursive = TRUE, full.names = TRUE)
round(sum(file.size(files)) / 1e6, 1)  # MB, both tiers
```

Because every lake is just another `lake_id=` partition, the same `out_root` can
hold many lakes, and `read_aeme_parquet()` (or DuckDB, Python, ...) can query them
all at once.

# Practical guidance

| Question | Guidance |
|---|---|
| How many members? | Cost is one full model run per member. Start with 10--20 to check the setup and the ranges, then increase until the quantiles you care about stop moving. Use `parallel = TRUE` for anything large. |
| What should the ranges be? | `min` and `max` *are* your prior. Overly wide ranges produce unphysical members (see *Members that fail*), which are dropped, so you pay for runs you cannot use; narrow them to what is physically defensible for the lake. |
| Sampled or supplied? | Sample from the bounds for exploration and as a prior. Supply parameter sets (e.g. a PEST++ posterior) when you want to propagate calibrated uncertainty. |
| Which output to keep? | `output_raw` keeps everything and lets you recompute anything later; `output_summary` is smaller and quicker for overviews, but its depths are scaled to each member's water level and so do not line up across members -- interpolate depth-resolved variables to fixed depths from the raw tier. |
| What does the spread mean? | Only parameter uncertainty. Forcing, initial conditions and structural error are not represented; for the initial state see `vignette("initial-conditions-and-spin-up")`. |
